'''asterid''' (as′tẹ-rid), ''n.'' [< ''Asteridæ.''] A starfish; a member of the genus ''Asterias'', or family ''Asteriidæ'', or some other division of the order ''Asteroidea''. Also called ''asteridan'' and ''asteridian''.

'''Asterida''' (as-ter′i-dä), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Asterias'', 1, + -''ida''.] In Gegenbaur’s system of classification, an order of the class ''Asteroida'', including the typical starfishes.

'''Asteridæ''' (as-ter′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Asterias'', 1, + -''idæ''.] '''1.''' Same as ''Asteriidæ''.—'''2.''' Some superfamily group of starfishes, more or less exactly equivalent to ''Asteroidea'' (which see).

'''asteridan''' (as-ter′i-dan), ''n.'' Same as ''asterid''.

'''Asteridea''' (as-tẹ-rid′ẹ̄-ä̤), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Asterias'', 1, + -''idea''.] A superfamily group of starfishes.
{{smaller block|(''a'') More or less nearly the same as an order ''Asteroidea'', distinguishing the starfishes collectively from other echinoderms. (''b'') More or less nearly the same as a class ''Asteroidea'' or ''Stellerida'', distinguishing the starfishes and sand-stars (ophiurians) together from other echinoderms.}}

'''asteridian''' (as-tẹ-rid′i-a̤n), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< ''asterid'' + -''ian''.] '''I.''' ''n.'' Same as ''asterid''.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the ''Asteriidæ''.
{{smaller block|The ''asteridian'' affinities of the class [''Brachiopoda''] have been hinted at by King.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', IV. 188.}}}}

'''asteriid''' (as-tē′ri-id), ''n.'' A starfish of the fam-

ily ''Asteriidæ.''

'''Asteriidæ''' (as-tẹ-rī′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Asterias'', 1, + ''-idæ''.] A family of echinoderms, of
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{smaller|Cross-section of ray of ''Asterias aurantiacus.''}}}}
{{c|{{smaller|''a, a,'' ambulacral or vertebral ossicles; ''b,'' adambulacral; ''c, c,'' marginal ossicles; ''d,'' paxillæ upon antambulacral surface.}}}}
the order ''Asteroidea'', the starfishes, class ''Asteroidea'' or ''Stellerida'', represented by such genera as ''Asterias'' or ''Astropecten'' and ''Luidia'', having four rows of pedicellate feet in each ray. Also ''Asteridæ'', and, less correctly, ''Asteriadæ.''

'''Asterina''' (as-tẹ-rī′nä), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀστήρ, a star, + ''-ina''.] The typical genus of starfishes of the family ''Asterinidæ''. ''A. gibbosa'' is the gibbous starlet.
{{smaller block|''Asterina'' is a large genus, almost world-wide in its distribution. The skeleton is formed of imbricated or overlapping and notched ossicula. {{right|''Stand. Nat. Hist.'', I. 159.}}}}

'''asterinid''' (as-ter′i-nid), ''n.'' A starlet of the family ''Asterinidæ.''

'''Asterinidæ''' (as-tẹ-rin′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Asterina'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of starfishes, containing the starlets of the genera ''Asterina'', ''Asteriscus'', ''Goniaster'', etc.

'''asterion''' (as-tē′ri-on), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀστέριος, neut. ἀστέριον, starry, starlike, < ἀστήρ, a star.] In ''anat.'', the point where the lambdoid, parietomastoid, and occipitomastoid sutures of the skull meet.

'''Asteriscus''' (as-te̤-ris′kus), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀστερίσκος, a little star: see ''asterisk.''] '''1.''' A genus of starfishes, of the family ''Asterinidæ'': synonymous with ''Palmipes.'' The species are known as sea-stars.—'''2.''' [''l. c.''] An otolith lodged, in most fishes, in a diverticulum of the vestibule, beneath the ampulla of the posterior canal.

'''asterisk''' (as′te̤-risk), ''n.'' [< LL. ''asteriscus,'' < Gr. ἀστερίσκος, a little star, an asterisk, used in manuscripts to mark passages, dim. of ἀστήρ, a star: see ''aster''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' The figure of a star (*), used in printing and writing—(''a'') as a reference to a passage or note in the margin; (''b'') to distinguish words or phrases as conjectural, theoretical, unverified, obscure, or as having some other specified character; (''c'') to mark the omission of words or letters; and (''d'') arbitrarily, as a mark of classification.—'''2.''' Something in the shape of or resembling an asterisk.
{{smaller block|The lanthorn is in the centre of an ''asterisk'' of glades, cut through the wood of all the country round, four or five in a quarter.
{{right|''Roger North,'' Lord Guilford, I. 258.}}}}

'''asternal''' (a-stėr′nạl), ''a.'' [< Gr. ἀ- priv. + στέρνον, sternum.] '''1.''' Having no sternum or breast-bone, as a serpent. [Rare.]—'''2.''' Not reaching to or connected with the sternum: as, ''asternal'' ribs, that is, floating ribs, ribs which do not articulate with the breast-bone.

'''Asterodactylidæ''' (as″te-rō-dak-til′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Asterodactylus'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of salient amphibians: synonymous with ''Pipidæ'' (which see). Also ''Asterodactyloidæ'' and ''Astrodactylidæ''.

'''Asterodactylus''' (as″te-rō-dak′ti-lus), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀστήρ, a star, + δάκτυλος, finger.] A genus of salient amphibians: synonymous with ''Pipa'' (which see).

'''asteroid''' (as′te-roid), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< Gr. ἀστεροειδής, star-like, < ἀστήρ, a star, + εἶδος, form.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Star-like.—'''2.''' Having a flower like that of an aster.

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' One of the small planets, 280 or more in number, between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter: more accurately called ''planetoids''. See ''planetoid''.—'''2.''' One of the ''Asteroidea''; a starfish, in a wide sense.

readings.c3s1:
{{smaller block|''terinidæ'', ''Goniasteridæ'', ''Linckiidæ'', and ''Asteriidæ'', or the starfishes proper as distinguished from the sand-stars and other echinoderms of the class ''Stellerida'' (which see). They have a coriaceous skin, in which are implanted spines or tubercles. The body is expanded into arms, the under surface of which is marked with grooves, radiating from the center, and pierced with rows of holes, whence issue tentacular feet, by means of which the animals move. Most have 5 arms or rays, but some have more, varying from 8 to 30. They have the power of reproducing these arms if they are broken off; and if an entire arm, with a small portion of the body attached to it, is torn off, it forms a new and perfect animal. The mouth is in the inferior center of the rays, is not provided with teeth, and leads by a short gullet into a large stomach, from which a pair of lateral tubes are prolonged into each ray. A distinct intestine and anus may or may not be present. The animals feed chiefly on mollusks.}}
'''2.''' A class of echinoderms, containing the sand-stars or ophiurians together with the starfishes, and more or less exactly equivalent to ''Stellerida'' (which see).—'''3.''' Same as ''Alcyonaria''.
readings.c3s3:

'''asterophrydid''' (as″te̤-rof′ri-did), ''n.'' One of the ''Asterophrydidæ.''

'''Asterophrydidæ''' (as″te̤-rō-frid′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Asterophrys'' + ''-idæ.''] A family of arciferous salient amphibians with maxillary teeth, dilated sacral diapophyses (the coccyx being connected with one or two condyles or sacral vertebræ), and opisthocœlian vertebræ. It is a small group of toad-like animals.

'''Asterophrys''' (as-te̤-rof′ris), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀστήρ, a star, + ὀφρύς, eyebrow: see ''brow.''] A genus of arciferous amphibians of New Guinea, typical of the family ''Asterophrydidæ.''

'''asterophyllite''' (as″te̤-rō-fil′īt), ''n.'' [< NL. ''Asterophyllites.''] A member of the genus ''Asterophyllites.''

'''Asterophyllites''' (as″te̤-rō-fi-lī′tēz), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀστήρ, a star, + φύλλον, a leaf, + λίθος, a stone.] A genus of fossil plants; star-leaf: so called from the stellated disposition of the leaves around the branches. {{smaller|They abound in the coal-measures, and are believed to be the branches of the ''Calamites'' or ''Calamodendron.''}}

'''astert†''', ''v.'' See ''astart.''

'''asthenia''' (as-the-nī′ä̤), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀσθένεια, weakness, < ἀσθενής, without strength, < ἀ- priv. + σθένος, strength.] '''1.''' In ''pathol.'', debility; want of strength. Also ''astheny.''—'''2.''' [''cap.''] In ''zoöl.'', a genus of insects.

'''asthenic''' (as-then′ik), ''a.'' [< Gr. ἀσθενικός, weak, < ἀσθενής: see ''asthenia.''] Of the nature of asthenia; characterized by or suffering from asthenia or debility; weak.

'''asthenology†''' (as-the-nol′ọ̄-ji), ''n.'' [< Gr. ἀσθενής, weak (see ''asthenia''), + -λογία, < λέγειν, speak: see ''-ology.''] The doctrine of diseases connected with debility.

'''asthenopia''' (as-the-nō′pi-ä̤), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀσθενής, weak (see ''asthenia''), + ὤψ (ὠπ-), eye.] Weakness of the eyes. {{smaller|Two forms are especially important: (''a'') ''accommodative asthenopia'', which is the result of the exhaustion of the ciliary muscle, as in hypermetropia; and (''b'') ''muscular asthenopia'', which is the result of some exhaustion of the external muscles of the eye, usually the internal rectus.}}

'''asthenopic''' (as-the-nop′ik), ''a.'' Pertaining to, resembling, or suffering from asthenopia.
{{smaller block|For reading, the manifest hypermetropia should be corrected, the strength of the glasses being increased as often as ''asthenopic'' symptoms reappear.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XVII. 785.}}}}

'''Asthenurus''' (as-the-nū′rus), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀσθενής, weak (see ''asthenia''), + οὐρά, tail.] '''1.''' In ''ornith.'', a genus of woodpeckers: synonymous with ''Picumnus. Swainson'', 1827.—'''2.''' In ''ichth.'', a genus of fishes.
readings.c3s5:

'''astheny''' (as′the-ni), ''n.'' Same as ''asthenia'', 1.

'''asthma''' (ast′mä or as′mä), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''astma'', ''asma'', < ME. ''asma'', ''asmy'', < ML. ''asma'', ''asthma'', < Gr. ἆσθμα, asthma, panting, < ἄζειν, also ἀάζειν, αἰάζειν, breathe hard, pant, < ἀῆναι (*''Fαῆναι''), breathe, blow, = Goth. ''waian'' = AS. ''wāwan'' = OHG. ''wājan'', MHG. ''wæjen'', G. ''wehen'' = Skt. √ ''vā'', blow. From the same root, in Gr., come
